name: Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
func: Controls one eye muscle, the superior oblique, which helps the eye look down and inward and rotates it inward. You use it when you look down to read or walk downstairs.

levels.kid:
The **trochlear nerve** is the thinnest wire that runs from your brain to your eye. It has just one job: it tells one small eye muscle to pull.

That muscle helps your eye look **down**, like when you look at your shoes or read a book on your lap. It also helps keep the picture **level** when you tip your head to the side.

Here is something fun: the muscle goes through a tiny loop of tissue, like a rope through a **pulley**. The word "trochlear" actually means "pulley." So this is the pulley nerve!
levels.hs:
The **trochlear nerve** is the fourth cranial nerve (**CN IV**). It is the **smallest** cranial nerve by number of axons, and it has the **longest path inside the skull**.

Two unique facts make it famous:
1. It is the only cranial nerve that **exits the back** of the brainstem, just below the **inferior colliculi** of the midbrain.
2. It is the only cranial nerve whose fibers **fully cross** to the other side before leaving the brain. So the left trochlear nucleus controls the right eye's muscle.

After exiting, it curves around the side of the midbrain, runs forward between the **posterior cerebral** and **superior cerebellar arteries**, pierces the edge of the **tentorium**, travels in the lateral wall of the **cavernous sinus** just below CN III, and enters the orbit through the **superior orbital fissure**, outside the tendinous ring.

It supplies the **superior oblique** muscle. The muscle's tendon runs through a fibrous loop, the **trochlea**, on the upper inner corner of the orbit, then turns back to attach to the eyeball. That lets it pull the eye **down** (especially when the eye is turned inward) and **rotate** the top of the eye toward the nose.
levels.college:
The **trochlear nucleus** lies in the caudal midbrain, at the level of the **inferior colliculus**, just ventral to the periaqueductal gray and embedded in the dorsal edge of the **medial longitudinal fasciculus**. Fibers run dorsally and caudally, then cross in the **superior medullary velum** (the roof of the upper fourth ventricle) before exiting.

The nerve's long, thin course around the midbrain in the **ambient cistern**, close to the free edge of the **tentorium cerebelli**, makes it vulnerable to shearing in head trauma.

Actions of the **superior oblique** depend on eye position because of the trochlea. Its main actions are **intorsion** (rotating the top of the eye toward the nose), **depression** and slight **abduction**. Its depressing action is strongest when the eye is **adducted**, so the clinical test is to ask the patient to look **down and in**. The opposite muscle partner for torsion is the inferior oblique (CN III).

In the orbit, CN IV runs above the levator and enters the superior oblique on its upper surface. It is the only extraocular motor nerve to pass through the superior orbital fissure **outside** the common tendinous ring, together with the frontal and lacrimal nerves.

Because of the decussation, a **nuclear or fascicular** lesion (inside the midbrain, before crossing) affects the **opposite** eye, while a lesion of the nerve after it exits affects the **same** side eye.
levels.phd:
Why does CN IV cross dorsally? Developmentally, trochlear motor axons grow dorsally from a ventral position in the midbrain–hindbrain region, steered by **netrin-1** repulsion acting through **Unc5c** and by **Slit/Robo** signaling at the dorsal midline. Mouse studies show these axons cross the dorsal midline in the anterior medullary velum, a rare route for motor axons.

Evolutionarily, the superior oblique and its crossed innervation are conserved across jawed vertebrates. One hypothesis links the crossing to the vestibular origins of torsional eye movements: vestibulo-ocular pathways from the semicircular canals must reach motor neurons that rotate the eye to stabilize gaze during head tilt, and the pattern of crossings may reflect the ancestral alignment of the eye muscles with the canal planes.

Torsional control has its own circuitry. The **interstitial nucleus of Cajal** and the **riMLF** encode vertical and torsional eye position and saccades, and **ocular counter-roll** during head tilt depends on otolith inputs from the utricle. Disruption of graviceptive pathways causes the **ocular tilt reaction**, which combines head tilt, skew deviation and ocular torsion, and can mimic a trochlear palsy.

Congenital superior oblique palsy is common. Many cases show an **absent or hypoplastic trochlear nerve** on high-resolution MRI, suggesting a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder, while others have tendon or muscle abnormalities. Patients often compensate for years by tilting the head, with large vertical fusional amplitudes, before decompensating in adulthood.
levels.expert:
A **CN IV palsy** is the most common cause of acquired **vertical double vision**. Patients complain of difficulty walking **downstairs** or reading. The affected eye sits **higher** (hypertropia), and they often **tilt the head away** from the affected side to reduce the double vision. Old photos showing a long-standing head tilt suggest a congenital, decompensated palsy.

The **Parks–Bielschowsky three-step test**:
1. Which eye is higher in primary gaze?
2. Is the deviation worse on looking to the right or to the left? (worse on gaze **away** from the affected eye)
3. Is it worse with head tilt to the right or left? (worse with tilt **toward** the affected side)

A **double Maddox rod** test measures excyclotorsion; more than about 10 degrees suggests a **bilateral** palsy, which is typical after severe head trauma because the two nerves cross close together in the superior medullary velum.

Causes: **head trauma** (the most common acquired cause), microvascular ischemia, congenital palsy, and less often tumors, **cavernous sinus** disease or aneurysm. A **skew deviation** from a brainstem or cerebellar lesion can mimic it; a vertical deviation that lessens when the patient lies down favors skew.

Neurosurgically, CN IV is at risk in **tentorial** and **pineal region** approaches and in tumors of the ambient cistern; surgeons identify and protect it during subtemporal and supracerebellar exposures. Management of persistent symptoms includes **prism** glasses and **strabismus surgery** (for example weakening the overacting inferior oblique).

keyPoints: CN IV: smallest cranial nerve, longest intracranial course
Only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem and to cross completely
Supplies the superior oblique: intorsion, depression (best in adduction)
Palsy → vertical double vision, trouble going downstairs, head tilt away
Head trauma is the most common acquired cause

test.q: The trochlear nerve supplies which muscle?
test.explain: CN IV supplies only the superior oblique, whose tendon runs through the trochlea.

test.q: CN IV exits from which surface of the brainstem?
test.explain: It is the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally, below the inferior colliculi.

test.q: A patient with a right CN IV palsy usually tilts their head:
test.explain: Tilting away from the affected side reduces the need for intorsion and lessens the double vision.

test.q: Patients with a trochlear palsy typically struggle most with:
test.explain: Looking down and in uses the superior oblique, so stairs and reading cause vertical diplopia.

test.q: The most common acquired cause of a CN IV palsy is head ______.
test.explain: The long thin nerve near the tentorial edge is easily injured in head trauma.
